frontalis: Skin of the eyebrows and forehead
Raises the eyebrows; wrinkles the forehead
Frontal belly of occipitofrontalis. All muscles of facial expression = CN VII.
occipitalis: Lateral superior nuchal line of the occipital bone; mastoid
Facial nerve (CN VII), posterior auricular branch
Occipital belly of occipitofrontalis; works with frontalis through the aponeurosis.
temporalis: Floor of the temporal fossa and temporal fascia
Coronoid process and anterior ramus of the mandible
Elevates the mandible; posterior fibres retract it
Mandibular nerve (CN V3), deep temporal branches
Muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter, both pterygoids) are all CN V3.
masseter: Zygomatic arch (inferior border and medial surface)
Lateral surface of the ramus and angle of the mandible
Elevates the mandible (closes the jaw); superficial part protracts
Palpate it at the jaw angle when you clench.
medial-pterygoid: Medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate; maxillary tuberosity
Medial surface of the ramus and angle of the mandible
Elevates and protrudes the mandible; side-to-side grinding
Forms a sling around the mandibular angle with masseter.
lateral-pterygoid: Upper head: greater wing of sphenoid. Lower head: lateral surface of lateral pterygoid plate
Neck of the mandible; articular disc and capsule of the TMJ
Protrudes and depresses the mandible (opens jaw); side-to-side movement
The only muscle of mastication that opens the mouth.
orbicularis-oculi: Medial orbital margin, medial palpebral ligament, lacrimal bone
Skin around the orbit; lateral palpebral raphe
Closes the eyelids (palpebral: blink; orbital: squeeze shut)
Facial nerve (CN VII), temporal and zygomatic branches
Loss of eye closure is a hallmark of Bell’s palsy.
orbicularis-oris: Maxilla and mandible near the midline; fibres of surrounding facial muscles
Skin and mucous membrane of the lips
Closes and protrudes the lips (kissing, whistling)
Facial nerve (CN VII), buccal and marginal mandibular branches
buccinator: Alveolar processes of maxilla and mandible; pterygomandibular raphe
Angle of the mouth (blends with orbicularis oris)
Presses the cheek against the teeth; keeps food between molars; blowing
Trumpeter’s muscle. Despite the name, NOT supplied by the buccal nerve of V3 (that one is sensory).
zygomaticus-major: Draws the angle of the mouth up and back (smiling)
depressor-anguli: Draws the angle of the mouth down (frowning)
Facial nerve (CN VII), marginal mandibular branch
mentalis: Elevates and wrinkles the chin; protrudes the lower lip (pouting)
nasalis: Maxilla above the incisors and canine
Nasal cartilages and the aponeurosis over the nose
risorius: Draws the angle of the mouth laterally (grimace)
corrugator: Medial end of the superciliary arch
Draws the eyebrows medially and down (frowning)
platysma: Fascia over pectoralis major and deltoid
Mandible, skin of the lower face and angle of the mouth
Tenses the skin of the neck; depresses the mandible and lower lip
A thin sheet in the superficial fascia of the neck.
scm: Sternal head: manubrium. Clavicular head: medial third of clavicle
Mastoid process and lateral superior nuchal line
One side: laterally flexes neck to same side and rotates face to opposite side. Both: flex the neck; accessory inspiration
Divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles. Torticollis involves a shortened SCM.
digastric: Anterior belly: digastric fossa of mandible. Posterior belly: mastoid notch of temporal bone
Intermediate tendon attached to the hyoid by a fibrous loop
Depresses the mandible; elevates the hyoid
Anterior belly: CN V3 (nerve to mylohyoid). Posterior belly: CN VII
Two bellies, two nerves — a favourite exam question.
mylohyoid: Body of the hyoid; median raphe
Forms the floor of the mouth; elevates the hyoid and tongue
stylohyoid: Styloid process of the temporal bone
geniohyoid: Inferior mental spine of the mandible
Pulls the hyoid forward and up; depresses the mandible
sternothyroid: Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
thyrohyoid: Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
Body and greater horn of the hyoid
Depresses the hyoid; raises the larynx when the hyoid is fixed
omohyoid: Superior border of the scapula near the suprascapular notch
Two bellies joined by an intermediate tendon; divides the neck triangles.
scalene-ant: Anterior tubercles of transverse processes C3–C6
Elevates the 1st rib (inspiration); flexes and laterally bends the neck
Key landmark: the brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass BEHIND it; the phrenic nerve runs ON it.
scalene-med: Posterior tubercles of transverse processes C2–C7
Superior surface of the 1st rib behind the subclavian groove
Elevates the 1st rib; laterally flexes the neck
The brachial plexus emerges between anterior and middle scalenes (interscalene triangle).
scalene-post: Posterior tubercles of transverse processes C4–C6
Elevates the 2nd rib; laterally flexes the neck
longus-colli: Bodies of C5–T3 and transverse processes C3–C5
Anterior tubercle of atlas, bodies of C2–C4, transverse processes C5–C6
Deep prevertebral muscle; important in whiplash.
longus-capitis: Anterior tubercles of transverse processes C3–C6
Basilar part of the occipital bone
splenius-capitis: Mastoid process and lateral superior nuchal line
Both: extend head and neck. One: laterally flexes and rotates the face to the SAME side
Posterior rami of middle cervical nerves
Superficial layer of the deep (intrinsic) back muscles.
splenius-cervicis: Extends the neck; rotates to the same side
Posterior rami of lower cervical nerves
levator-scapulae: Medial border of the scapula above the spine
Elevates the scapula; rotates the glenoid downward
Shrug with a downward-rotation twist — tight in people who carry bags on one shoulder.
rcp-major: Extends the head; rotates the face to the same side
oc-superior: Occipital bone between the nuchal lines
Extends and laterally flexes the head
oc-inferior: Rotates the atlas (and head) to the same side
The only “capitis” muscle that does not attach to the skull.
semispinalis: Occipital bone (capitis) and spinous processes of cervical/upper thoracic vertebrae
Extends head and vertebral column; rotates to the opposite side
trapezius: External occipital protuberance, superior nuchal line, nuchal ligament, spinous processes C7–T12
Lateral third of the clavicle, acromion, spine of the scapula
Upper: elevates scapula. Middle: retracts. Lower: depresses. Upper + lower: upward rotation for overhead reach
Accessory nerve (CN XI) motor; C3–C4 sensory
Test: shrug against resistance. Injury to CN XI in the posterior triangle → drooping shoulder.
lats: Spinous processes T7–T12, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, lower 3–4 ribs, inferior angle of scapula
Floor of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus
Extends, adducts and medially rotates the humerus (pull-ups, rowing)
“A lady between two majors”: pectoralis major (lateral lip), latissimus (floor), teres major (medial lip).
rhomboid-major: Medial border of the scapula below the spine
Retracts the scapula; rotates the glenoid downward; fixes scapula to thoracic wall
rhomboid-minor: Medial border of the scapula at the root of the spine
Retracts and downwardly rotates the scapula
iliocostalis: Iliac crest, sacrum, angles of ribs
Angles of ribs and transverse processes of cervical vertebrae
Extends and laterally flexes the vertebral column
Erector spinae, lateral column. Lateral → medial: “I Love Spaghetti” (Iliocostalis, Longissimus, Spinalis).
longissimus: Common erector spinae tendon; transverse processes
Extends and laterally flexes the vertebral column and head
Erector spinae, intermediate column; the largest.
spinalis: Spinous processes of upper lumbar and lower thoracic vertebrae
Spinous processes of upper thoracic and cervical vertebrae
multifidus: Sacrum, ilium, transverse processes T1–T12, articular processes C4–C7
Thickest in the lumbar region; key segmental stabiliser in low-back rehab.
quadratus-lumborum: Laterally flexes the trunk; fixes 12th rib in inspiration; hip hiking
levatores-costarum: Ribs just below (breves) or two below (longi)
interspinales: Superior surface of a spinous process
Inferior surface of the spinous process above
pec-major: Clavicular head: medial clavicle. Sternocostal head: sternum, costal cartilages 1–6. Abdominal part: rectus sheath
Lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus
Adducts and medially rotates the humerus; clavicular head flexes, sternocostal head extends from flexion
pec-minor: Stabilises scapula by pulling it anteroinferiorly; elevates ribs in forced inspiration
Landmark that divides the axillary artery into 3 parts; tightness can compress the cords (pec minor syndrome).
subclavius: Junction of 1st rib and costal cartilage
Inferior surface of the middle clavicle
Cushions the plexus and subclavian vessels in clavicle fractures.
serratus-anterior: Anterior surface of the medial border of the scapula
Protracts the scapula and rotates it upward; holds it against the thoracic wall
Injury → medial winging of the scapula (push against a wall).
ext-intercostal: Inferior border of the rib above
Superior border of the rib below (fibres run down and forward)
Elevate the ribs in forced inspiration
Fibres run like hands in pockets, same as the external oblique.
int-intercostal: Inferior border of the rib above (costal groove)
Superior border of the rib below (fibres at right angles to externals)
Depress the ribs in forced expiration (interosseous part)
innermost-intercostal: Costal groove of the rib above
Superior border of the rib below
The intercostal neurovascular bundle (VAN, top to bottom) runs between internal and innermost layers.
transversus-thoracis: Posterior surface of the lower sternum
diaphragm: Xiphoid process, costal cartilages 7–12, lumbar vertebrae L1–L3 via the crura
Primary muscle of inspiration: contracts and descends, enlarging the thoracic cavity
“C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive.” Referred pain to the shoulder tip.
rectus-abdominis: Flexes the trunk; compresses the abdominal viscera; posterior pelvic tilt
Tendinous intersections create the “six-pack”; enclosed in the rectus sheath.
ext-oblique: Linea alba, pubic tubercle, anterior half of the iliac crest
Both: flex trunk and compress abdomen. One: laterally flexes and rotates trunk to the OPPOSITE side
Its inferior aponeurotic edge forms the inguinal ligament.
int-oblique: Thoracolumbar fascia, anterior iliac crest, lateral inguinal ligament
Inferior borders of ribs 10–12, linea alba, pubis via conjoint tendon
Flexes trunk; compresses abdomen; rotates trunk to the SAME side
Thoracoabdominal nerves, T12, L1 (iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal)
Fibres run at right angles to the external oblique.
transversus-abdominis: Internal surfaces of costal cartilages 7–12, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, inguinal ligament
Linea alba, pubic crest via conjoint tendon
Compresses the abdomen; stabilises the lumbar spine
Deepest flat abdominal muscle; horizontal fibres act like a corset.
levator-ani: Body of the pubis, tendinous arch of obturator fascia, ischial spine
Supports the pelvic viscera; resists rises in intra-abdominal pressure; puborectalis maintains faecal continence
Nerve to levator ani (S4), pudendal nerve branches
coccygeus: Supports pelvic viscera; flexes the coccyx
deltoid: Lateral third of the clavicle, acromion, spine of the scapula
Anterior: flexes and medially rotates. Middle: abducts (15–90°). Posterior: extends and laterally rotates
Axillary nerve injury (surgical-neck fracture, shoulder dislocation) → weak abduction and numb “regimental badge” patch.
supraspinatus: Superior facet of the greater tubercle
SITS rotator cuff. Most commonly torn cuff tendon (impingement under the acromion).
infraspinatus: Middle facet of the greater tubercle
Laterally rotates the humerus; cuff stabiliser
teres-minor: Middle part of the lateral border of the scapula
Inferior facet of the greater tubercle
Laterally rotates the humerus; cuff stabiliser
SITS. Teres minor is cuff; teres major is not.
subscapularis: Medially rotates and adducts the humerus; cuff stabiliser
The only SITS muscle on the lesser tubercle.
teres-major: Posterior surface of the inferior angle of the scapula
Medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus
Adducts and medially rotates the humerus
“Lat’s little helper.” Forms borders of the quadrangular and triangular spaces.
coracobrachialis: Middle third of the medial humerus
biceps-brachii: Short head: coracoid process. Long head: supraglenoid tubercle
Supinates the forearm (strongest action); flexes the elbow; weakly flexes the shoulder
Biceps reflex tests C5–C6. Long head tendon runs in the intertubercular sulcus.
brachialis: Distal half of the anterior humerus
Coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna
Flexes the elbow in all positions (the “workhorse”)
Inserts on the ulna, so it cannot supinate.
triceps: Long head: infraglenoid tubercle. Lateral head: posterior humerus above radial groove. Medial head: below radial groove
Extends the elbow; long head extends and adducts the shoulder
Triceps reflex tests C7. Radial nerve runs in the groove between lateral and medial heads.
anconeus: Assists elbow extension; stabilises the elbow
pronator-teres: Humeral head: medial epicondyle. Ulnar head: coronoid process
Middle of the lateral surface of the radius
Pronates the forearm; assists elbow flexion
Median nerve passes between its two heads (pronator syndrome).
fcr: Flexes and radially deviates the wrist
Radial pulse is just lateral to its tendon.
palmaris-longus: Flexes the wrist; tenses palmar aponeurosis
Absent in ~14% of people; used for tendon grafts.
fcu: Humeral head: medial epicondyle. Ulnar head: olecranon and posterior ulna
Pisiform, hook of hamate, base of 5th metacarpal
Only superficial flexor supplied by the ulnar nerve. Ulnar nerve enters the forearm between its heads (cubital tunnel).
fds: Humeroulnar head: medial epicondyle and coronoid. Radial head: anterior radius
Intermediate layer of the anterior forearm. Test: hold other fingers straight, flex one PIP.
fdp: Anterior and medial ulna; interosseous membrane
Flexes DIP joints (the only muscle that does)
Medial half: ulnar nerve. Lateral half: anterior interosseous (median)
Dual innervation — “one and a half muscles” of the forearm flexors are ulnar (FCU + half FDP).
fpl: Base of the distal phalanx of the thumb
pronator-quadratus: Deepest muscle of the distal anterior forearm.
brachioradialis: Proximal two-thirds of the lateral supracondylar ridge
Lateral distal radius just above the styloid
Flexes the elbow, especially in mid-pronation
An elbow FLEXOR supplied by the radial nerve — the odd one out.
ecrl: Extends and radially deviates the wrist
Wrist extension is essential for a strong grip.
ecrb: Extends and radially deviates the wrist
The tendon most involved in lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow).
ext-digitorum: Extends the fingers at MCP and IP joints; extends the wrist
ecu: Lateral epicondyle and posterior border of ulna
supinator: Lateral epicondyle, radial collateral and annular ligaments, supinator crest of ulna
Lateral, posterior and anterior surfaces of proximal radius
The deep radial nerve passes through it and becomes the posterior interosseous nerve.
apl: Posterior ulna, radius and interosseous membrane
Abducts and extends the thumb at the CMC joint
Forms the lateral border of the anatomical snuffbox (with EPB). De Quervain’s tenosynovitis.
epb: Base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb
epl: Posterior middle third of the ulna and interosseous membrane
Base of the distal phalanx of the thumb
Medial border of the anatomical snuffbox; hooks around Lister’s tubercle.
ext-indicis: Extensor expansion of the index finger
apb: Flexor retinaculum, scaphoid and trapezium tubercles
Lateral base of the thumb proximal phalanx
Recurrent branch of the median nerve (C8–T1)
Thenar wasting is a late sign of carpal tunnel syndrome.
fpb: Lateral base of thumb proximal phalanx
Superficial head: median (recurrent). Deep head: ulnar
opponens-pollicis: Opposes the thumb (rotates it to meet the fingers)
Recurrent branch of the median nerve
Opposition is what makes the human hand special.
adductor-pollicis: Oblique head: capitate and bases of 2nd–3rd metacarpals. Transverse head: anterior 3rd metacarpal
Medial base of the thumb proximal phalanx
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
Froment’s sign tests it (ulnar nerve palsy).
adm-hand: Medial base of the proximal phalanx of digit 5
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve
fdmb-hand: Hook of hamate and flexor retinaculum
Medial base of the proximal phalanx of digit 5
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve
odm-hand: Hook of hamate and flexor retinaculum
Draws the 5th metacarpal forward to meet the thumb
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve
lumbricals-hand: Lateral sides of the extensor expansions of digits 2–5
Flex MCP joints and extend IP joints (“table-top” position)
Same split as FDP, because they arise from its tendons.
dorsal-interossei-hand: Extensor expansions and proximal phalanges of digits 2–4
ABduct the fingers (DAB); flex MCP, extend IP
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve
“DAB and PAD”: Dorsal ABduct, Palmar ADduct.
palmar-interossei: Extensor expansions and proximal phalanges of digits 2, 4, 5
ADduct the fingers (PAD); flex MCP, extend IP
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve
Grip a sheet of paper between your fingers to test them.
psoas-major: Transverse processes, bodies and discs T12–L5
Flexes the hip (with iliacus = iliopsoas); flexes and laterally bends the lumbar spine
The femoral nerve emerges from its lateral border; the obturator nerve from its medial border.
iliacus: Iliac fossa, iliac crest, ala of sacrum
Flexes the hip; stabilises the hip joint
Iliopsoas is the strongest hip flexor.
glute-max: Posterior ilium, dorsal sacrum and coccyx, sacrotuberous ligament
Iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosity of the femur
Extends the thigh (rising from sitting, climbing); laterally rotates; steadies the knee via IT tract
Largest muscle in the body. Injections go in the upper-outer quadrant to avoid the sciatic nerve.
glute-med: External ilium between anterior and posterior gluteal lines
Lateral surface of the greater trochanter
Abducts and medially rotates the thigh; keeps the pelvis level in single-leg stance
Weakness → positive Trendelenburg sign (opposite hip drops).
glute-min: External ilium between anterior and inferior gluteal lines
Anterior surface of the greater trochanter
Abducts and medially rotates the thigh; levels the pelvis
tfl: Iliotibial tract (to lateral condyle of tibia)
Abducts, medially rotates and flexes the thigh; stabilises the extended knee
piriformis: Anterior surface of the sacrum; sacrotuberous ligament
Superior border of the greater trochanter
Laterally rotates the extended thigh; abducts the flexed thigh
KEY landmark of the gluteal region: superior gluteal nerve exits ABOVE it; sciatic and inferior gluteal BELOW it.
obturator-int: Pelvic surface of the obturator membrane and surrounding bone
Laterally rotates the thigh; holds the femoral head in the acetabulum
Exits the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen.
obturator-ext: External surface of the obturator membrane
Classified with the medial (adductor) compartment by innervation.
quadratus-femoris: Lateral border of the ischial tuberosity
sartorius: Flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the hip; flexes the knee (cross-legged)
Longest muscle in the body. Forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle.
rectus-femoris: AIIS and ilium above the acetabulum
Base of patella → tibial tuberosity via patellar ligament
Extends the knee; flexes the hip
Only quadriceps muscle crossing the hip.
vastus-lateralis: Greater trochanter and lateral lip of the linea aspera
vastus-medialis: Intertrochanteric line and medial lip of the linea aspera
Extends the knee; VMO stabilises the patella medially
adductor-longus: Body of the pubis below the crest
Middle third of the linea aspera
Medial border of the femoral triangle. Classic groin strain.
adductor-brevis: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis
Pectineal line and proximal linea aspera
The anterior and posterior branches of the obturator nerve lie on either side of it.
adductor-magnus: Adductor part: inferior pubic ramus and ischial ramus. Hamstring part: ischial tuberosity
Gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera, adductor tubercle
Adducts the thigh; adductor part flexes, hamstring part extends
Adductor part: obturator. Hamstring part: tibial division of sciatic
Adductor hiatus lets femoral vessels pass to become popliteal.
gracilis: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis
Adducts the thigh; flexes and medially rotates the knee
Pes anserinus: “Say Grace before Tea” — Sartorius, Gracilis, semiTendinosus.
biceps-femoris: Long head: ischial tuberosity. Short head: linea aspera
Flexes the knee and laterally rotates the flexed leg; long head extends the hip
Long head: tibial division. Short head: common fibular division of sciatic
Lateral hamstring. The common fibular nerve follows its tendon to the fibular head.
semitendinosus: Flexes the knee; extends the hip; medially rotates the flexed leg
Long tendon used for ACL grafts.
semimembranosus: Posterior medial condyle of the tibia
Flexes the knee; extends the hip; medially rotates the flexed leg
tibialis-anterior: Lateral condyle and upper lateral tibia; interosseous membrane
Medial cuneiform and base of 1st metatarsal
Foot drop / high-stepping gait after common fibular nerve injury at the fibular neck.
ehl: Middle anterior fibula and interosseous membrane
Base of the distal phalanx of the big toe
Extends the big toe; dorsiflexes the ankle
edl: Lateral tibial condyle, proximal fibula, interosseous membrane
Middle and distal phalanges of toes 2–5
fibularis-tertius: Part of EDL; absent in some.
fibularis-longus: Base of 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform (via the sole)
Everts and weakly plantarflexes the foot; supports arches
Tendon runs behind the lateral malleolus and under the cuboid.
fibularis-brevis: Everts and weakly plantarflexes the foot
Avulsion of the 5th metatarsal base in ankle inversion injuries.
gastrocnemius: Lateral head: lateral femoral condyle. Medial head: popliteal surface above medial condyle
Plantarflexes the ankle; flexes the knee
Ankle reflex tests S1. Forms triceps surae with soleus.
soleus: Posterior head of fibula, soleal line of tibia, tendinous arch
Plantarflexes the ankle; postural muscle (prevents falling forward)
Calf-muscle pump (“peripheral heart”) for venous return.
plantaris: Lateral supracondylar line of the femur
popliteus: Lateral femoral condyle and lateral meniscus
Posterior tibia above the soleal line
Unlocks the knee (medially rotates tibia / laterally rotates femur)
tibialis-posterior: Posterior tibia, fibula and interosseous membrane
Navicular tuberosity, cuneiforms, cuboid, bases of metatarsals 2–4
Plantarflexes and inverts the foot; supports the medial arch
Tarsal tunnel order behind medial malleolus: “Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry” (Tib post, FDL, artery, vein, nerve, FHL).
fdl: Posterior tibia below the soleal line
fhl: Distal phalanx of the big toe
Flexes the big toe; push-off in walking
Deepest tendon in the tarsal tunnel.
edb: Only muscle on the dorsum of the foot (with EHB).
ehb: Base of the proximal phalanx of the big toe
Extends the big toe MTP joint
abductor-hallucis: Medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity, flexor retinaculum
Medial base of the big toe proximal phalanx
Abducts and flexes the big toe
adm-foot: Lateral base of the 5th toe proximal phalanx
quadratus-plantae: Corrects the oblique pull of FDL
fhb: Both sides of the base of the big toe proximal phalanx
Flexes the big toe MTP joint
Plantar layer 3; sesamoid bones sit in its tendons.
adductor-hallucis: Oblique head: bases of metatarsals 2–4. Transverse head: plantar MTP ligaments
Lateral base of the big toe proximal phalanx
Adducts the big toe; supports the transverse arch
Deep branch of lateral plantar nerve
fdmb-foot: Base of the 5th toe proximal phalanx
lumbricals-foot: Medial sides of the extensor expansions of toes 2–5
Flex MTP and extend IP joints
plantar-interossei: Medial bases of proximal phalanges of toes 3–5
ADduct toes 3–5 (toward the 2nd toe); flex MTP
dorsal-interossei-foot: ABduct toes 2–4 (from the 2nd toe axis); flex MTP

epicranial-apo: Tough aponeurosis linking frontalis and occipitalis over the vault of the skull.
Scalp layers: Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose areolar tissue, Pericranium (SCALP).
linea-alba: Midline fibrous seam from xiphoid to pubic symphysis where the aponeuroses of the three flat abdominal muscles interlace.
Relatively avascular — a classic surgical incision line.
inguinal-lig: Folded inferior edge of the external oblique aponeurosis from the ASIS to the pubic tubercle.
The femoral nerve, artery and vein pass beneath it (NAVeL, lateral to medial).
interosseous-membrane-forearm: Fibrous sheet binding the radius and ulna; transmits force from radius to ulna.
flexor-retinaculum: Transverse carpal ligament bridging the carpal arch to form the roof of the carpal tunnel.
Contents: median nerve + 9 tendons (4 FDS, 4 FDP, FPL). Compression = carpal tunnel syndrome.
it-tract: Thickened lateral band of the fascia lata, receiving TFL and gluteus maximus, inserting on the lateral tibial condyle (Gerdy’s tubercle).
IT band friction syndrome in runners.
calcaneal-tendon: Common tendon of gastrocnemius, soleus (and plantaris) inserting on the posterior calcaneus.
Thickest, strongest tendon in the body. Thompson test: squeeze the calf — no plantarflexion means rupture.
interosseous-membrane-leg: Fibrous sheet between tibia and fibula separating anterior and posterior compartments.
Muscles of both compartments arise from it.
long-plantar-lig: Ligament from the plantar calcaneus to the cuboid and bases of metatarsals 2–5.
Main passive support of the lateral longitudinal arch.

frontal: Forms the forehead, roof of the orbits and anterior cranial fossa.
Supraorbital foramen/notch; coronal suture with parietals.
parietal: Paired bones forming the roof and sides of the cranium.
Sagittal, coronal, lambdoid and squamous sutures.
temporal: Houses the middle and inner ear; forms part of the side and base of the skull.
Mastoid process (SCM), styloid process, zygomatic process, mandibular fossa (TMJ), external acoustic meatus, stylomastoid foramen (CN VII).
occipital: Forms the posterior skull and much of the base.
Foramen magnum, occipital condyles (atlanto-occipital joint), external occipital protuberance, superior/inferior nuchal lines.
sphenoid: Butterfly-shaped keystone of the cranial base.
Sella turcica (pituitary), greater/lesser wings, pterygoid plates (pterygoid muscles), foramen ovale (CN V3).
ethmoid: Light, spongy bone between the orbits forming part of the nasal septum and roof.
Cribriform plate (olfactory nerves), crista galli, perpendicular plate, superior/middle conchae.
zygomatic: Zygomatic arch with the temporal bone (origin of masseter).
maxilla: Upper jaw; forms the orbit floor, nasal cavity walls and hard palate.
Alveolar process, infraorbital foramen, maxillary sinus.
nasal: Small paired bones forming the bridge of the nose.
lacrimal: Smallest facial bone, in the medial orbit wall.
Lacrimal fossa for the tear sac.
palatine: L-shaped bones forming the posterior hard palate.
concha: Scroll-like bones on the lateral nasal walls that warm and humidify air.
vomer: Forms the inferior part of the nasal septum.
mandible: Lower jaw; the only movable skull bone.
Body, ramus, angle, coronoid process (temporalis), condylar process (TMJ), mental foramen. TMJ is a synovial hinge/gliding joint with an articular disc.
hyoid: U-shaped bone suspended in the neck; articulates with no other bone.
Attachment for supra- and infrahyoid muscles and the tongue.
thyroid-cart: Hyaline cartilage; attachment of sternothyroid and thyrohyoid.
atlas: C1: ring-shaped, no body or spinous process.
Atlanto-occipital joint (“yes” nodding); atlanto-axial joint (“no” rotation).
axis: Dens is the pivot for atlanto-axial rotation (pivot joint).
cervical: C3–C7: small bodies, bifid spinous processes, transverse foramina (vertebral artery).
thoracic: T1–T12: heart-shaped bodies, costal facets for ribs, long downward spinous processes.
Thoracic kyphosis. Costovertebral and costotransverse joints.
lumbar: L1–L5: large kidney-shaped bodies, short thick spinous processes.
Lumbar lordosis; spinal cord ends at L1–L2 (conus medullaris).
sacrum: Five fused vertebrae forming the posterior pelvis.
Sacroiliac joints, sacral foramina (S1–S4 nerves), sacral promontory.
discs: Fibrocartilaginous pads between vertebral bodies: outer annulus fibrosus + inner nucleus pulposus.
Symphysis (secondary cartilaginous) joints. Posterolateral herniation compresses spinal nerve roots.
manubrium: Jugular notch, clavicular notches (sternoclavicular joint), sternal angle at rib 2 (T4/T5 level).
xiphoid: Small inferior tip of the sternum; cartilaginous in youth.
Attachment for diaphragm and rectus abdominis. CPR hand position avoids it.
ribs: 12 pairs. True ribs 1–7 (own cartilage to sternum), false 8–10, floating 11–12.
Head, neck, tubercle, angle, costal groove (intercostal neurovascular bundle).
costal-cart: Hyaline cartilage joining ribs to the sternum.
clavicle: S-shaped strut between sternum and scapula.
Sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints. Most commonly fractured bone (middle third).
scapula: Flat triangular bone of the shoulder girdle.
Spine, acromion, coracoid process, glenoid cavity, supra-/infraspinous fossae, subscapular fossa, supra-/infraglenoid tubercles.
humerus: Head, anatomical and surgical necks (axillary nerve), greater/lesser tubercles, intertubercular sulcus, deltoid tuberosity, radial groove (radial nerve), medial epicondyle (ulnar nerve), capitulum, trochlea.
radius: Head (proximal radioulnar pivot joint), radial tuberosity (biceps), styloid process, Lister’s tubercle.
ulna: Olecranon (triceps), coronoid process (brachialis), trochlear notch (elbow hinge), styloid process.
carpals: Eight wrist bones in two rows.
Proximal: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform. Distal: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate (“Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can’t Handle”). Scaphoid fractures risk avascular necrosis.
metacarpals: 1st CMC joint is a saddle joint (opposition).
phalanges-hand: 14 finger bones: thumb has 2, other digits 3.
hip-bone: Os coxae: fused ilium, ischium and pubis meeting at the acetabulum.
Iliac crest, ASIS, AIIS, PSIS, greater sciatic notch, ischial tuberosity (hamstrings), obturator foramen, pubic symphysis, acetabulum (ball-and-socket hip joint).
femur: Head, neck, greater/lesser trochanters, linea aspera, adductor tubercle, medial/lateral condyles. Knee is a modified hinge joint.
patella: Largest sesamoid bone, in the quadriceps tendon.
Increases the lever arm of the quadriceps.
tibia: Tibial plateau, tibial tuberosity (patellar ligament), medial malleolus, soleal line.
fibula: Thin lateral leg bone; mostly for muscle attachment.
Head, neck (common fibular nerve wraps around it), lateral malleolus.
tarsals: Talus (ankle hinge with tibia/fibula), calcaneus (heel), navicular, cuboid, three cuneiforms.
metatarsals: Five long bones of the foot.
phalanges-foot: 14 toe bones: big toe has 2, others 3.

spinal-cord: Continuous with the medulla at the foramen magnum
Runs in the vertebral canal from the foramen magnum to about L1–L2 (conus medullaris); 31 pairs of spinal nerves leave through intervertebral foramina.
Contains upper motor neuron tracts; anterior horn lower motor neurons supply all skeletal muscle below the head.
Cord ends at L1–L2, so lumbar punctures are done at L3–L4 or L4–L5.
cauda-equina: Bundle of lumbar, sacral and coccygeal nerve roots descending in the vertebral canal below the conus.
Roots of the lumbar and sacral plexuses.
Cauda equina syndrome: saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction — emergency.
brachial-plexus: Roots → trunks (upper, middle, lower) → divisions → cords (lateral, posterior, medial) → terminal branches. Emerges between anterior and middle scalenes, passes behind the clavicle into the axilla.
“Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer” = Roots, Trunks, Divisions, Cords, Branches.
Erb’s palsy (C5–C6, “waiter’s tip”); Klumpke’s palsy (C8–T1, claw hand).
musculocutaneous: Pierces coracobrachialis, runs between biceps and brachialis, becomes the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
Weak elbow flexion and supination; numb lateral forearm.
median: Medial arm with the brachial artery → cubital fossa → between FDS and FDP → through the carpal tunnel → thenar muscles and lateral fingers.
Most anterior forearm flexors (except FCU and medial FDP), thenar muscles, lumbricals 1–2.
Carpal tunnel syndrome: numb thumb–index–middle fingers, thenar wasting, “ape hand”. High lesion → “hand of benediction”.
ulnar: Medial arm → behind the medial epicondyle (“funny bone”) → between FCU heads → beside the ulnar artery → Guyon’s canal → hand.
FCU, medial half of FDP, hypothenar muscles, interossei, lumbricals 3–4, adductor pollicis, deep head of FPB.
Claw hand (ring and little fingers), weak finger abduction/adduction, Froment’s sign.
radial: Through the triangular interval, spirals in the radial groove of the humerus between triceps heads, then anterior to the lateral epicondyle; splits into deep (posterior interosseous) and superficial branches.
All posterior arm and forearm muscles: triceps, anconeus, brachioradialis, wrist and finger extensors, supinator.
Mid-shaft humerus fracture → wrist drop (can’t extend wrist or fingers).
axillary: Passes through the quadrangular space and wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus.
Surgical-neck fracture or shoulder dislocation → weak abduction, flattened shoulder, numb “regimental badge” area.
long-thoracic: Descends behind the plexus on the outer surface of serratus anterior along the lateral chest wall.
Injury (e.g. mastectomy, heavy backpacks) → medially winged scapula.
suprascapular: Passes through the suprascapular notch under the superior transverse scapular ligament, then around the spinoglenoid notch.
Weak initiation of abduction and lateral rotation.
dorsal-scapular: Pierces middle scalene, runs deep to levator scapulae and the rhomboids along the medial border of the scapula.
Levator scapulae, rhomboid major and minor.
Weak scapular retraction; lateral scapular winging.
thoracodorsal: Runs down the posterior axillary wall into the deep surface of latissimus dorsi.
Weak extension/adduction of the arm (pull-ups, climbing).
subscapular: Upper and lower subscapular nerves on the posterior axillary wall.
Upper: subscapularis. Lower: subscapularis and teres major.
pectoral: Lateral C5–C7 (lateral cord); medial C8–T1 (medial cord)
Lateral pectoral pierces the clavipectoral fascia; medial pectoral pierces pectoralis minor.
Named for the cord they come from, not their position (medial pectoral is actually more lateral).
accessory: Exits the jugular foramen, passes through/deep to SCM, crosses the posterior triangle, ends deep to trapezius.
Injury in the posterior triangle (lymph-node biopsy) → drooping shoulder, weak shrug.
facial: Exits the stylomastoid foramen, passes through the parotid gland and fans out as 5 branches: Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical (“To Zanzibar By Motor Car”).
All muscles of facial expression; posterior digastric, stylohyoid.
Bell’s palsy: one-sided facial paralysis, can’t close the eye or smile on that side.
mandibular: Exits the skull through the foramen ovale into the infratemporal fossa.
Muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter, pterygoids), anterior digastric, mylohyoid.
Jaw deviates toward the paralysed side when opening.
phrenic: Descends on the anterior surface of anterior scalene, enters the thorax, runs between pericardium and pleura to the diaphragm.
“C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive.” High cervical cord injury stops breathing.
intercostal: Run in the costal groove between internal and innermost intercostals (VAN order: vein, artery, nerve). T7–T11 continue into the abdominal wall; T12 is the subcostal nerve.
Intercostal muscles; T7–T12 supply the anterolateral abdominal muscles.
Dermatomes: T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus. Shingles follows one intercostal dermatome.
femoral: Emerges lateral to psoas, runs between psoas and iliacus, passes under the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery (NAVeL), branches in the femoral triangle; the saphenous branch continues to the medial leg.
Anterior thigh: quadriceps, sartorius, pectineus, iliacus.
Weak knee extension, lost patellar reflex (L3–L4).
obturator: Emerges medial to psoas, runs along the lateral pelvic wall, exits through the obturator canal; anterior and posterior branches straddle adductor brevis.
Medial thigh: adductors longus, brevis, magnus (adductor part), gracilis, obturator externus.
sciatic: Largest nerve in the body. Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen BELOW piriformis, descends between the greater trochanter and ischial tuberosity, deep to biceps femoris; divides into tibial and common fibular above the popliteal fossa.
Hamstrings and hamstring part of adductor magnus; everything below the knee via its divisions.
Misplaced gluteal injection or posterior hip dislocation → sciatic injury. Sciatica = compressed L4–S1 roots.
tibial: Through the popliteal fossa, deep to gastrocnemius and soleus, behind the medial malleolus in the tarsal tunnel; splits into medial and lateral plantar nerves.
Posterior leg (gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris, popliteus, tibialis posterior, FDL, FHL) and all plantar foot muscles.
Can’t plantarflex or stand on tiptoe; tarsal tunnel syndrome.
common-fibular: Follows biceps femoris tendon, wraps around the NECK OF THE FIBULA (very superficial), splits into superficial fibular (lateral compartment) and deep fibular (anterior compartment, dorsum of foot).
Short head of biceps femoris; anterior compartment (dorsiflexors) via deep fibular; lateral compartment (evertors) via superficial fibular.
Most commonly injured nerve of the lower limb: fibular neck fracture, tight cast, crossing legs → foot drop, steppage gait.
superior-gluteal: Leaves the pelvis ABOVE piriformis, runs between gluteus medius and minimus to TFL.
Gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensor fasciae latae.
inferior-gluteal: Leaves the pelvis BELOW piriformis, enters the deep surface of gluteus maximus.
Difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs.
pudendal: Leaves through the greater sciatic foramen, hooks around the ischial spine, re-enters via the lesser sciatic foramen into the perineum (pudendal canal).
External anal and urethral sphincters, perineal muscles, parts of levator ani.
“S2, 3, 4 keeps the pelvis off the floor.” Pudendal nerve block in childbirth.

BELL: A volleyball player feels a sharp pain at the top of the RIGHT shoulder and now cannot START lifting the arm away from the body, although once someone lifts it past 30° she can continue. Find the injured muscle.
Shoulder — posterior scapula, above the spine
Rotator cuff; suprascapular nerve; initiates abduction 0–15°
Supraspinatus initiates abduction; the deltoid takes over after ~15°. It is the most commonly torn cuff tendon.

After a fall onto the LEFT shoulder, an X-ray shows a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus. The patient has a numb patch over the lateral shoulder and weak abduction. Find the nerve that was injured.
Wraps around the back of the humeral neck
Quadrangular space; supplies deltoid + teres minor
The axillary nerve wraps around the surgical neck; injury weakens deltoid and numbs the “regimental badge” area.
A carpenter has a mid-shaft fracture of the RIGHT humerus and cannot extend the wrist — the hand hangs limp. Locate the nerve running in the groove where the bone broke.
Posterior arm, spiralling around the humerus
Radial nerve in the radial (spiral) groove → wrist drop.
A data-entry clerk has tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers of the RIGHT hand that wakes her at night. Find the nerve passing through the carpal tunnel.
Median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel = carpal tunnel syndrome.
A student hits the “funny bone” on the inside of the LEFT elbow and feels electric tingling into the little finger. Find the nerve.
Medial cord C8–T1; supplies most intrinsic hand muscles
The ulnar nerve is unprotected behind the medial epicondyle.
After a mastectomy that included axillary node removal, the patient’s RIGHT scapula sticks out like a wing when she pushes against a wall. Find the paralysed muscle.
Lateral chest wall, over the ribs
Long thoracic nerve; protracts the scapula
Serratus anterior paralysis (long thoracic nerve) → medial winging.
A rock climber struggles to pull himself up — the strongest arm extensor/adductor on his LEFT side is weak. It inserts in the floor of the intertubercular sulcus. Find it.
Broad muscle of the lower back
Latissimus dorsi extends, adducts and medially rotates the humerus.
A tennis player has pain over the lateral epicondyle of the RIGHT elbow when gripping. Find the wrist extensor most often involved.
Arises from the common extensor origin; inserts on 3rd metacarpal
Extensor carpi radialis brevis is most implicated in lateral epicondylitis.
A weightlifter feels a pop in the front of the LEFT arm and now has weak SUPINATION — turning a doorknob is hard. Find the muscle.
Musculocutaneous nerve; inserts on the radial tuberosity
Biceps brachii is the most powerful supinator.
A patient cannot flex the tip (DIP joint) of any finger on the RIGHT hand. Find the only muscle that flexes the DIP joints.
Flexor digitorum profundus inserts on the distal phalanges.
A runner with weak hip abductors: when he stands on his RIGHT leg, the LEFT side of the pelvis drops (positive Trendelenburg). Find the weak muscle.
Lateral hip, under the gluteus maximus edge
Superior gluteal nerve; levels the pelvis
Weakness of the stance-side gluteus medius lets the opposite hip drop.
A man fractured the neck of the LEFT fibula playing soccer. His foot slaps the ground and he lifts his knee high to clear his toes. Find the injured nerve.
Divides into superficial and deep branches
Common fibular nerve injury at the fibular neck → foot drop.
With foot drop, which muscle in the anterior compartment of the RIGHT leg is the main dorsiflexor that has lost its nerve supply? Find it.
Front of the shin, lateral to the tibia
Deep fibular nerve; inserts on medial cuneiform
Tibialis anterior is the main dorsiflexor and inverter.
During a sprint, a sprinter feels a sudden “kick” at the back of the LEFT heel and can no longer rise onto his toes. The Thompson test is positive. Find the ruptured structure.
A nurse gives an injection into the lower inner part of the RIGHT buttock; the patient later has weakness of everything below the knee. Find the injured nerve.
Deep in the buttock, below piriformis
L4–S3; largest nerve in the body
The sciatic nerve exits below piriformis; injections go in the upper-outer quadrant to avoid it.
A soccer player strains a muscle in the LEFT groin while kicking. It forms the medial border of the femoral triangle. Find it.
Adductor longus is the classic “groin strain.”
A patient has difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a chair, but walking on level ground is normal. The powerful hip extensor on the RIGHT is weak. Find it.
Gluteus maximus is needed for forceful hip extension (stairs, rising).
The patellar tendon reflex on the LEFT is absent. Find the nerve carrying this reflex (L2–L4).
Under the inguinal ligament into the anterior thigh
Femoral nerve → quadriceps; patellar reflex tests L3–L4.
A pianist cannot spread (abduct) her fingers on the RIGHT hand. Find the muscle group responsible.
Between the metacarpals, back of the hand
A long-distance runner has lateral knee pain where a thick band of fascia rubs over the femoral condyle on the RIGHT. Find the structure.
A patient with a high spinal cord injury at C3 cannot breathe on her own. Find the nerve whose roots were affected (choose either side).
The phrenic nerve is the only motor supply to the diaphragm.
Find the primary muscle of inspiration that the phrenic nerve supplies.
Central tendon; crura on lumbar vertebrae
The diaphragm contracts and descends during inspiration.
After a lymph-node biopsy in the posterior triangle of the LEFT neck, the patient cannot shrug that shoulder. Find the muscle that lost its nerve.
Trapezius (upper fibres) elevate the scapula; CN XI crosses the posterior triangle.
A patient wakes with drooping of the LEFT side of the face and cannot close the LEFT eye. Find the nerve affected.
Exits in front of the ear through the parotid
Find the muscle that closes the eyelids — the one that fails in Bell’s palsy (RIGHT side).
A boxer is told to strengthen the jaw muscle he can feel bulging at the angle of the mandible when clenching (RIGHT). Find it.
Side of the face over the mandibular ramus
A patient with torticollis holds the head tilted to the RIGHT with the chin turned to the LEFT. Find the shortened muscle.
Side of the neck, sternum to mastoid
Right SCM tilts the head right and turns the face left.
A gymnast has low back pain from the large muscle column that extends the spine. Find the intermediate (largest) column of the erector spinae on the LEFT.
Longissimus is the intermediate erector spinae column.
A patient has a hernia bulging through the abdominal wall just above the inguinal ligament. Find the muscle whose aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament (RIGHT).
External oblique aponeurosis rolls under to form the inguinal ligament.
A swimmer has pain deep in the RIGHT buttock radiating down the back of the leg. The muscle suspected of compressing the sciatic nerve arises from the anterior sacrum. Find it.
Landmark: nerves exit above and below it
A patient cannot stand on tiptoe on the LEFT and has lost the ankle-jerk reflex (S1). Find the nerve that supplies the calf muscles.
Back of the knee, deep in the calf
Find the calf muscle that crosses BOTH the knee and ankle on the RIGHT (two heads, diamond shape).
Gastrocnemius flexes the knee and plantarflexes the ankle; soleus crosses only the ankle.
A patient with an old radial nerve injury cannot extend the elbow fully on the RIGHT. Find the elbow extensor.
A patient with thenar wasting from long-term carpal tunnel syndrome cannot touch the thumb to the little finger (RIGHT). Find the muscle that opposes the thumb.
A skier tears a ligament in the knee and the surgeon harvests a long tendon from a medial hamstring for the graft (LEFT). Find the muscle.
Pes anserinus; tibial division of sciatic
Semitendinosus tendon is a common ACL graft.
Find the longest muscle in the body, which you use to sit cross-legged (RIGHT).
Crosses the front of the thigh diagonally
A patient with a winged scapula that shifts LATERALLY has weak scapular retraction on the LEFT. Find the nerve to the rhomboids and levator scapulae.
Find the muscle that the median nerve passes between the two heads of, in the proximal RIGHT forearm.
Pronator teres; pronator syndrome compresses the median nerve here.
The intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove. Find the nerves that supply the intercostal muscles and the abdominal wall (either side).
Along the underside of each rib

heart: Pumps into the aorta (left ventricle) and pulmonary trunk (right ventricle)
Cardiac muscle: striated, branched, intercalated discs — compare with skeletal muscle physiology.
aorta: Ascending aorta → arch (brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian) → descending thoracic → abdominal aorta → bifurcates at L4
Largest artery. The arch hooks over the left main bronchus.
brachiocephalic-a: Right common carotid and right subclavian arteries
Right side of head, neck and right upper limb
common-carotid: Internal and external carotid at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4)
Carotid pulse beside the larynx, medial to SCM. Travels in the carotid sheath with the IJV and vagus nerve.
subclavian-a: Becomes the axillary artery at the outer border of the 1st rib
Upper limb, plus vertebral and internal thoracic arteries
Passes BEHIND anterior scalene with the brachial plexus (thoracic outlet).
coronary-a: Aortic sinuses just above the aortic valve
Right coronary (marginal, posterior interventricular) and left coronary (LAD, circumflex)
Blockage causes myocardial infarction; the LAD is the most commonly occluded.
pulmonary-a: The only arteries carrying deoxygenated blood (after birth).
pulmonary-v: Returns oxygenated blood from the lungs
Usually four veins, two per lung.
celiac: Left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries
Foregut: stomach, liver, spleen, pancreas, upper duodenum
sma: Midgut: small intestine to proximal two-thirds of transverse colon
ima: Left colic, sigmoid, superior rectal arteries
renal-a: The right renal artery passes behind the IVC.
external-iliac-a: Becomes the femoral artery under the inguinal ligament
internal-iliac-a: Gluteal, obturator, pudendal and visceral branches
Pelvic walls, viscera, gluteal region, perineum
ivc: Union of the common iliac veins at L5
Lies to the right of the aorta.
brachiocephalic-v: Two of them (left is longer); only one brachiocephalic artery.
internal-jugular: Central-line site; in the carotid sheath lateral to the carotid.
ijv-upper: Upper course traced for this app.
subclavian-v: Passes IN FRONT of anterior scalene (the artery passes behind).
renal-v: Left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta.
external-iliac-v: Femoral vein at the inguinal ligament
portal-tributaries: Join behind the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein
Abdominal GI tract and spleen (to the liver)
axillary-a: Becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major
Divided into 3 parts by pectoralis minor; surrounded by the cords of the brachial plexus.
brachial-a: Radial and ulnar arteries in the cubital fossa
Blood-pressure cuff artery; runs with the median nerve, medial to biceps.
radial-a: Brachial artery in the cubital fossa
Radial pulse lateral to the FCR tendon; floor of the anatomical snuffbox.
ulnar-a: Brachial artery in the cubital fossa
Runs with the ulnar nerve through Guyon’s canal. Allen test.
femoral-a: External iliac at the inguinal ligament
Becomes popliteal at the adductor hiatus
Femoral pulse at the mid-inguinal point; femoral triangle NAVeL (lateral → medial).
deep-femoral-a: Femoral artery in the femoral triangle
Perforating branches, medial and lateral circumflex femoral
Main blood supply of the thigh.
popliteal-a: Femoral artery at the adductor hiatus
Deepest structure in the popliteal fossa.
ant-tibial-a: Becomes dorsalis pedis at the ankle
Runs with the deep fibular nerve.
dorsalis-pedis: Pulse lateral to the EHL tendon.
post-tibial-a: Pulse behind the medial malleolus (tarsal tunnel).
internal-carotid: Enters skull via carotid canal; circle of Willis
external-carotid: Superior thyroid, lingual, facial, maxillary, superficial temporal, etc.
Facial pulse at the anterior border of masseter.
vertebral-a: Ascends through transverse foramina C6–C1 to form the basilar artery
brachial-v: Venae comitantes of the radial and ulnar arteries
Paired veins hugging the brachial artery.
cephalic: Lateral (thumb) side of the dorsal venous network
Axillary vein via the deltopectoral groove
Thumb side = cephalic; little-finger side = basilic.
basilic: Medial (little-finger) side of the dorsal venous network
Pierces deep fascia mid-arm to join the brachial veins → axillary vein
median-cubital: Standard venipuncture site in the cubital fossa.
femoral-v: Popliteal vein at the adductor hiatus
Deep veins of the lower limb
Medial to the femoral artery (NAVeL). Common DVT site.
great-saphenous: Medial dorsal venous arch, in front of the medial malleolus
Femoral vein at the saphenous opening
Longest vein in the body; harvested for bypass grafts; varicose veins.
small-saphenous: Lateral dorsal venous arch, behind the lateral malleolus
external-jugular: Behind the angle of the mandible
radial-v: Join the ulnar veins at the elbow to form the brachial veins
Venae comitantes: paired veins that hug the radial artery.
ulnar-v: Join the radial veins to form the brachial veins
Venae comitantes of the ulnar artery.
ant-tibial-v: Dorsal venous arch / dorsalis pedis veins
Join the posterior tibial veins to form the popliteal vein
post-tibial-v: Posterior compartment of the leg and sole
Deep calf veins are a common site of deep vein thrombosis (DVT); soleal venous sinuses drain into them.
fibular-v: Paired venae comitantes of the fibular artery.
deep-femoral-v: Lies anterior to the deep femoral artery.
dorsal-venous-hand: Cephalic vein (thumb side) and basilic vein (little-finger side)
The visible veins on the back of your hand; common IV site.
palmar-venous-arch: Superficial and deep arches run with the arterial arches.
median-antebrachial: Variable; runs up the middle of the anterior forearm.
ant-circ-humeral-v: Front of the surgical neck of the humerus
Runs with the anterior circumflex humeral artery.
post-circ-humeral-v: Travels with the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery through the quadrangular space.
subscapular-v: Subscapular fossa and infraspinous fossa (circumflex scapular)
Circumflex scapular vessels pass through the triangular space.
thoracodorsal-v: Runs with the thoracodorsal nerve and artery.
lateral-thoracic-v: Follows the long thoracic nerve region.
suprascapular-v: Passes ABOVE the superior transverse scapular ligament (the nerve passes below).
anterior-jugular: The two anterior jugular veins are linked by the jugular venous arch above the sternum.
facial-v: Connects with the cavernous sinus — the “danger triangle” of the face.
retromandibular-v: Superficial temporal + maxillary veins, behind the mandible
Side of the face and scalp
Runs through the parotid gland with the facial nerve.
vertebral-v: Descends through the transverse foramina with the vertebral artery.
internal-thoracic-v: Superior epigastric veins in the rectus sheath
Anterior chest and upper abdominal wall
Runs just lateral to the sternum; anastomoses with the inferior epigastric veins.
inferior-epigastric-v: Lateral border of the inguinal (Hesselbach) triangle.
thoracoepigastric-v: A bypass between the SVC and IVC systems; dilates when the IVC is blocked.
lumbar-v: IVC; linked vertically by the ascending lumbar vein to the azygos/hemiazygos
sup-gluteal-v: Exit ABOVE piriformis with the superior gluteal nerve.
internal-pudendal-v: Runs in the pudendal canal with the pudendal nerve.
accessory-saphenous: Joins the great saphenous just below the saphenous opening.
perforating-v: One-way valves send blood deep; failure causes varicose veins.
dorsal-venous-arch: Great saphenous (medial end) and small saphenous (lateral end)
Visible on top of the foot.
azygos: Ascending lumbar vein / right subcostal vein at T12
Arches over the right lung root into the SVC at T4
Posterior thoracic and abdominal wall (right posterior intercostal veins)
Major collateral between SVC and IVC.
hemiazygos: Crosses behind the aorta to the azygos at about T8–T9
portal-v: Union of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins behind the pancreas
Blood from the gut is processed by the liver before reaching the heart.
hepatic-v: Inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm
testicular-v-R: Asymmetry explains why varicoceles are more common on the left.
testicular-v-L: Left: into the left renal vein (at a right angle)
Asymmetry explains why varicoceles are more common on the left.
post-intercostal-v: In the costal groove the order top to bottom is VAN: Vein, Artery, Nerve.
cardiac-veins: Coronary sinus (anterior cardiac veins drain directly into the right atrium)
coronary-sinus: Great, middle and small cardiac veins
Lies in the posterior coronary sulcus.
thoracoacromial-a: Acromial, deltoid, pectoral and clavicular branches; pierces the clavipectoral fascia
Mnemonic for the axillary branches: “Screw The Lawyer Save A Patient” — Superior thoracic, Thoracoacromial, Lateral thoracic, Subscapular, Anterior & Posterior circumflex humeral.
superior-thoracic-a: Small branch to the 1st–2nd intercostal spaces
Only branch of the 1st part of the axillary artery.
lateral-thoracic-a: Follows the lateral border of pectoralis minor
circumflex-scapular-a: Through the triangular space to the infraspinous fossa
thoracodorsal-a: Runs with the thoracodorsal nerve into latissimus dorsi
ant-circ-humeral-a: Winds in front of the surgical neck of the humerus
Shoulder joint, long head of biceps, deltoid
post-circ-humeral-a: Through the quadrangular space with the axillary nerve, around the surgical neck
Injured with the axillary nerve in surgical-neck fractures.
thyrocervical-trunk: Inferior thyroid, suprascapular and transverse cervical arteries
suprascapular-a: Passes OVER the superior transverse scapular ligament (nerve passes under) into the supra- and infraspinous fossae
“Army over the bridge, Navy under the bridge.”
transverse-cervical-a: Crosses the posterior triangle to trapezius
dorsal-scapular-a: Runs with the dorsal scapular nerve along the medial border of the scapula
costocervical-trunk: Deep cervical and superior intercostal arteries
Deep neck muscles, first two intercostal spaces
internal-thoracic-a: Runs behind the costal cartilages beside the sternum; ends as the superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries
Anterior chest wall, breast, diaphragm, upper rectus abdominis
Used for coronary artery bypass grafts.
profunda-brachii: Runs with the radial nerve in the radial groove
Triceps and the back of the arm
Endangered with the radial nerve in mid-shaft humerus fractures.
superior-ulnar-collateral: Runs with the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle
radial-recurrent: Runs up beside the lateral epicondyle
ulnar-recurrent: Anterior and posterior branches up beside the medial epicondyle
anterior-interosseous-a: Down the front of the interosseous membrane with the anterior interosseous nerve
Deep anterior forearm (FDP, FPL, pronator quadratus)
posterior-interosseous-a: Over the interosseous membrane to the back of the forearm
superficial-palmar-arch: Lies distal to the deep arch, at the level of the outstretched thumb.
genicular-a: Superior and inferior, medial and lateral genicular arteries
Form the genicular anastomosis around the knee.
sural-a: Into the two heads of gastrocnemius and soleus
plantar-a: Posterior tibial artery (behind the medial malleolus)
The lateral plantar artery forms the deep plantar arch
arcuate-a: Dorsum of the foot and toes
lingual-a: Tongue and floor of the mouth
facial-a: Crosses the mandible at the anterior border of masseter, toward the medial angle of the eye
Pulse felt where it crosses the mandible.
maxillary-a: External carotid artery (terminal branch) behind the mandibular neck
Middle meningeal and many other branches
Jaws, teeth, muscles of mastication, nasal cavity, meninges
superficial-temporal-a: In front of the ear to the temple
Pulse felt in front of the ear.
post-intercostal-a: Run in the costal groove below the vein, above the nerve (VAN)
Intercostal muscles, chest wall, spinal cord
superficial-epigastric-a: Up the superficial lower abdominal wall
superficial-circumflex-iliac-a: Skin and fascia of the lateral groin
descending-genicular-a: Femoral artery in the adductor canal
deep-circumflex-iliac-a: Along the iliac crest deep to the abdominal muscles
inferior-epigastric-a: Up behind rectus abdominis to anastomose with the superior epigastric
Medial to the deep inguinal ring — separates direct from indirect inguinal hernias.
obturator-a: Medial thigh (adductors), head of femur via the ligament of the head
circ-femoral-a: Deep artery of the thigh (or femoral artery)
Head and neck of the femur, thigh muscles
The medial circumflex femoral is the main supply of the femoral head — damaged in femoral neck fractures (avascular necrosis).

MNEM.supraspinatus: SITS = the rotator cuff: Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, Subscapularis. "Supraspinatus starts the swing" — it initiates abduction before deltoid takes over.
MNEM.infraspinatus: SITS rotator cuff. Infraspinatus + teres minor are the two lateral rotators of the cuff ("In and Tiny turn it out").
MNEM.teres-minor: SITS rotator cuff. Teres MINOR is a cuff muscle; teres MAJOR is not ("minor is in the cuff, major is the lat's little helper"). Axillary nerve, like deltoid.
MNEM.subscapularis: SITS rotator cuff — the only cuff muscle on the front of the scapula, so it is the only medial rotator of the four.
MNEM.teres-major: "Lat's little helper": same actions as latissimus (extend, adduct, medially rotate) and inserts beside it on the medial lip of the intertubercular groove.
MNEM.lats: "Lady between two Majors": in the intertubercular groove, latissimus (Lady) inserts on the floor between pectoralis major (lateral lip) and teres major (medial lip). The "swimmer's / chin-up muscle".
MNEM.pec-major: "Lady between two Majors" — pec major inserts on the LATERAL lip of the intertubercular groove.
MNEM.deltoid: Axillary nerve wraps the surgical neck of the humerus: surgical-neck fracture → flat shoulder and weak abduction past 15°.
MNEM.serratus-anterior: "Boxer's muscle" (protracts the scapula to punch). Long thoracic nerve injury → winged scapula. Long thoracic = C5, 6, 7 → "C5-6-7 raise your wings to heaven".
MNEM.trapezius: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) — test by shrugging. Cut in posterior-triangle surgery → drooping shoulder.
MNEM.rhomboid-major: Rhomboids: "Dorsal scapular for the rhomboids and levator" — they retract the scapula (squeeze your shoulder blades).
MNEM.rhomboid-minor: Rhomboid MINOR sits ABOVE major (minor = higher, smaller). Both: dorsal scapular nerve.
MNEM.levator-scapulae: Name says it: lifts the scapula. Dorsal scapular nerve + C3–C4.
MNEM.pec-minor: Landmark muscle: divides the axillary artery into parts 1, 2, 3 (above, behind, below it). "Screw The Lawyer Save A Patient" = branches: Superior thoracic (1), Thoracoacromial + Lateral thoracic (2), Subscapular + Anterior & Posterior circumflex humeral (3).
MNEM.biceps-brachii: "Biceps: the corkscrew muscle" — strongest supinator; you supinate to drive in a screw (right hand) and flex to pull the cork. Musculocutaneous nerve: "MC supplies BBC" = Biceps, Brachialis, Coracobrachialis.
MNEM.brachialis: "MC supplies BBC" (musculocutaneous → Biceps, Brachialis, Coracobrachialis). Brachialis is the pure elbow flexor — the workhorse.
MNEM.coracobrachialis: "MC supplies BBC". The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis — a classic exam fact.
MNEM.triceps: Radial nerve = "BEST": Brachioradialis, Extensors, Supinator, Triceps. Radial nerve runs in the radial (spiral) groove → mid-shaft humerus fracture → wrist drop.
MNEM.brachioradialis: "BEST" (radial nerve: Brachioradialis, Extensors, Supinator, Triceps). The "beer-drinking muscle": flexes the elbow best in mid-pronation.
MNEM.anconeus: Tiny triangle at the back of the elbow — radial nerve, helps triceps.
MNEM.pronator-teres: Superficial flexors, lateral to medial: "Pete Frank Plays Football" = Pronator teres, Flexor carpi radialis, Palmaris longus, Flexor carpi ulnaris (FDS lies just deep). Trick: put the heel of your opposite hand on the medial epicondyle — your four fingers fan out in the same order.
MNEM.fcr: "Pete Frank Plays Football" — Pronator teres, Flexor carpi radialis, Palmaris longus, Flexor carpi ulnaris. All from the common flexor origin (medial epicondyle).
MNEM.palmaris-longus: Absent in about 14% of people — touch thumb to little finger and flex the wrist to see if you have one. Its tendon is a favourite graft.
MNEM.fcu: "Ulnar nerve: 1½ muscles in the forearm" — FCU and the medial half of FDP. Everything else in the anterior forearm = median.
MNEM.fds: "FDS splits to let FDP pass": the superficialis tendon splits (Sublimis Splits) at the middle phalanx so the profundus tendon can go through to the distal phalanx.
MNEM.fdp: "FDP = Profundus to the Pad of the distal phalanx". Dual supply: lateral half median (anterior interosseous), medial half ulnar.
MNEM.fpl: Anterior interosseous nerve (median) → "OK sign" test: weak FPL + FDP index make a pinch look like a flat "pinch".
MNEM.pronator-quadratus: Deepest muscle at the front of the wrist; square shape = quadratus. Anterior interosseous nerve.
MNEM.ecrl: Extensor compartments at the wrist (lateral → medial, 1–6): "APL EPB / ECRL ECRB / EPL / ED EI / EDM / ECU" — remember "2-2-1-2-1-1" tendons per compartment.
MNEM.ecrb: Lateral epicondylitis ("tennis elbow") = inflammation of the common extensor origin, classically ECRB.
MNEM.ext-digitorum: Extensor compartment 4 carries extensor digitorum + extensor indicis. All posterior forearm muscles = radial nerve ("BEST").
MNEM.apl: Anatomical snuffbox borders: APL + EPB laterally, EPL medially. Radial artery and scaphoid lie in the floor ("Snuffbox tenderness = scaphoid fracture").
MNEM.epb: Snuffbox lateral border (with APL). De Quervain tenosynovitis = APL + EPB in compartment 1.
MNEM.epl: Snuffbox medial border. Hooks around Lister's tubercle on the radius.
MNEM.supinator: "BEST" (radial nerve). The deep branch of the radial nerve (posterior interosseous) pierces supinator.
MNEM.ecu: Compartment 6 — ulnar side of the wrist; with FCU it adducts (ulnar deviates) the wrist.
MNEM.apb: Thenar muscles "A-F-O-A": Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis, Opponens pollicis (all median, recurrent branch) + Adductor pollicis (ulnar). Median injury → ape hand.
MNEM.opponens-pollicis: "LOAF" = median nerve in the hand: Lateral two Lumbricals, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis.
MNEM.fpb: "LOAF" (median: Lumbricals 1–2, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis).
MNEM.adductor-pollicis: The odd one out of the thumb — ULNAR nerve. Froment's sign: a weak adductor makes the patient flex the thumb (FPL) to hold paper.
MNEM.lumbricals-hand: Lumbricals: flex the MCP, extend the IP joints ("hold a playing card"). Lateral two = median (LOAF), medial two = ulnar.
MNEM.dorsal-interossei-hand: "PAD and DAB": Palmar ADduct, Dorsal ABduct. All interossei = ulnar nerve (test: spread the fingers against resistance).
MNEM.palmar-interossei: "PAD and DAB": Palmar interossei ADduct the fingers toward the middle finger. Ulnar nerve.
MNEM.adm-hand: Hypothenar "A-F-O" mirrors the thenar group: Abductor, Flexor, Opponens digiti minimi — all ulnar nerve.
MNEM.iliocostalis: Erector spinae lateral → medial: "I Love Spaghetti" = Iliocostalis, Longissimus, Spinalis.
MNEM.longissimus: "I Love Spaghetti" — Longissimus is the middle (and longest) column of erector spinae.
MNEM.spinalis: "I Love Spaghetti" — Spinalis is the most medial column, hugging the spinous processes.
MNEM.multifidus: Transversospinalis deep group "Some Men Run" = Semispinalis, Multifidus, Rotatores (superficial → deep).
MNEM.semispinalis: "Some Men Run" (Semispinalis, Multifidus, Rotatores). Semispinalis capitis forms the big rope either side of the nuchal midline.
MNEM.quadratus-lumborum: "QL = the hip hiker": hitches the pelvis up on one side; also anchors the 12th rib during breathing.
MNEM.splenius-capitis: Splenius = "bandage" — wraps over the deep neck muscles like a bandage.
MNEM.scm: Divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles. CN XI. Torticollis (wry neck) = shortened SCM: head tilts toward, face turns away.
MNEM.scalene-ant: "Anterior scalene: the phrenic nerve rides on its front". Subclavian VEIN passes in front of it, subclavian ARTERY + brachial plexus pass behind (between anterior and middle scalenes).
MNEM.scalene-med: The brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass between the anterior and middle scalenes (interscalene triangle).
MNEM.digastric: "Two bellies, two nerves": anterior belly = CN V3 (mylohyoid nerve), posterior belly = CN VII.
MNEM.omohyoid: "Omo" = shoulder: runs from the scapula to the hyoid, with a tendon held by a fascial sling. Ansa cervicalis supplies the strap muscles.
MNEM.sternohyoid: Infrahyoid "strap" muscles: Sternohyoid, Sternothyroid, Thyrohyoid, Omohyoid — all ansa cervicalis (C1–C3) except thyrohyoid (C1 via XII).
MNEM.platysma: Facial nerve (cervical branch) — a muscle of facial expression that lives in the neck.
MNEM.masseter: Muscles of mastication = CN V3: "M-T-P-P" Masseter, Temporalis, Medial & Lateral Pterygoid. Lateral pterygoid is the only one that OPENS the jaw.
MNEM.temporalis: Mastication (CN V3). Posterior fibres retract the mandible.
MNEM.lateral-pterygoid: "Lateral Lowers" — the only mastication muscle that depresses (opens) the jaw and protrudes it.
MNEM.medial-pterygoid: Mirrors the masseter on the inside of the ramus — a sling that closes the jaw.
MNEM.buccinator: "Trumpeter muscle" — keeps food between the teeth. Facial nerve, even though it is pierced by the parotid duct.
MNEM.orbicularis-oculi: Facial nerve. Bell's palsy → cannot close the eye on that side.
MNEM.frontalis: All muscles of facial expression = CN VII ("Two Zebras Bit My Cookie" = Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical branches).
MNEM.diaphragm: "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive" — phrenic nerve. Openings: "I 8 10 Eggs AT 12" = IVC T8, oEsophagus T10, Aorta T12.
MNEM.ext-intercostal: "Hands in pockets": external intercostals run down and forward like your fingers in front pockets (inspiration). Internals run at right angles.
MNEM.int-intercostal: Internal intercostals run at right angles to the externals ("hands on your chest"); forced expiration. The neurovascular bundle runs below the rib: VAN (Vein, Artery, Nerve) top to bottom.
MNEM.ext-oblique: "Hands in pockets" fibre direction, like external intercostals. Its lower edge rolls under to form the inguinal ligament.
MNEM.int-oblique: Fibres run at right angles to the external oblique (up and medial). Forms the conjoint tendon with transversus.
MNEM.transversus-abdominis: Deepest flat abdominal muscle — horizontal fibres, a corset. Three flat muscles: External, Internal, Transversus ("E-I-T" outside → in).
MNEM.rectus-abdominis: Tendinous intersections make the "six-pack". Enclosed in the rectus sheath; linea alba between the two recti.
MNEM.glute-max: Inferior gluteal nerve. Main hip extender for climbing stairs and standing up — not much used in normal walking.
MNEM.glute-med: Superior gluteal nerve. Trendelenburg sign: weak gluteus medius → pelvis DROPS on the opposite side when standing on the affected leg ("the sound side sags").
MNEM.glute-min: Superior gluteal nerve, with glute medius and TFL ("superior gluteal = Med, Min, TFL").
MNEM.tfl: Superior gluteal nerve; pulls on the IT band to stabilise the extended knee.
MNEM.piriformis: Key landmark of the gluteal region: everything is named "above or below piriformis". Sciatic nerve usually exits BELOW it. Lateral rotators: "P-GO-GO-Q" = Piriformis, Gemellus superior, Obturator internus, Gemellus inferior, Obturator externus, Quadratus femoris.
MNEM.obturator-int: "P-GO-GO-Q" (Piriformis, Gemellus sup., Obturator int., Gemellus inf., Obturator ext., Quadratus femoris) — the short lateral rotators, top to bottom.
MNEM.sartorius: "Tailor's muscle" — crossing your legs to sew uses all its actions (flex, abduct, laterally rotate hip; flex knee). Pes anserinus: "Say Grace before Tea" = Sartorius, Gracilis, semiTendinosus insert on medial tibia.
MNEM.gracilis: "Say Grace before Tea" — Sartorius, Gracilis, semiTendinosus form the pes anserinus (goose foot) on the medial tibia.
MNEM.semitendinosus: "Say Grace before Tea" (pes anserinus). Semi-TENDINosus has the long cord-like TENDON; semimembranosus is the flat membrane deep to it.
MNEM.semimembranosus: Lies deep to semitendinosus — "the tendon sits on the membrane". Hamstrings = tibial part of sciatic, except the short head of biceps femoris (common fibular).
MNEM.biceps-femoris: Lateral hamstring. Long head: tibial division; short head: common fibular division — the only hamstring part not crossing the hip.
MNEM.rectus-femoris: The only quadriceps muscle that crosses the hip (flexes it). Quads = femoral nerve (L2–L4) → knee-jerk reflex L3–L4.
MNEM.vastus-medialis: "VMO" teardrop above the medial knee — keeps the patella tracking centrally.
MNEM.adductor-longus: Femoral triangle borders "SAIL": Sartorius, Adductor longus, Inguinal Ligament. Contents lateral → medial "NAVeL": Nerve, Artery, Vein, (empty space), Lymphatics.
MNEM.adductor-magnus: Two-part muscle: adductor part (obturator nerve) + hamstring part (tibial nerve). The adductor hiatus lets the femoral vessels become popliteal.
MNEM.psoas-major: Iliopsoas = strongest hip flexor. Lumbar plexus (L1–L3) branches emerge from psoas — "the plexus is born inside psoas".
MNEM.iliacus: Femoral nerve to iliacus; with psoas forms iliopsoas onto the lesser trochanter.
MNEM.tibialis-anterior: Anterior compartment "Tom, Harry and Dick" — Tibialis anterior, (extensor) Hallucis longus, (extensor) Digitorum longus — all deep fibular nerve. Weakness → foot drop (high-stepping gait).
MNEM.ehl: "Tom HARRY and Dick" (anterior leg). Deep fibular nerve.
MNEM.edl: "Tom, Harry and DICK" (anterior leg). Deep fibular nerve; fibularis tertius is a slip of it.
MNEM.fibularis-longus: Lateral compartment = superficial fibular nerve; evertors. Longus crosses under the foot to the 1st metatarsal — "stirrup" with tibialis anterior.
MNEM.fibularis-brevis: Superficial fibular nerve. Inserts on the 5th metatarsal tuberosity (avulsion fracture in inversion sprains).
MNEM.gastrocnemius: Triceps surae = gastrocnemius (2 heads) + soleus → calcaneal (Achilles) tendon. Tibial nerve, S1–S2 → ankle jerk "S1, 2 buckle my shoe".
MNEM.soleus: "The second heart": soleus venous pump returns blood from the leg. Soleus works when the knee is bent (gastrocnemius is slack).
MNEM.tibialis-posterior: Behind the medial malleolus "Tom, Dick ANd Very Nervous Harry": Tibialis posterior, Digitorum (FDL), Artery, Vein, Nerve (tibial), Hallucis (FHL).
MNEM.fdl: "Tom, DICK And Very Nervous Harry" — FDL second behind the medial malleolus.
MNEM.fhl: "Tom, Dick And Very Nervous HARRY" — FHL is last (most posterior-lateral) behind the medial malleolus.
MNEM.popliteus: "Unlocks the knee": laterally rotates the femur on the tibia at the start of flexion.
MNEM.plantaris: Long thin tendon ("freshman's nerve" — often mistaken for a nerve in lab). Absent in some people.
MNEM.abductor-hallucis: First layer of the sole (with FDB and ADM). Medial plantar nerve.
MNEM.brachial-plexus: "Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer" = Roots, Trunks, Divisions, Cords, Branches (5-3-6-3-5). Terminal branches "MARMU": Musculocutaneous, Axillary, Radial, Median, Ulnar.
MNEM.musculocutaneous: "MC supplies BBC" — Biceps, Brachialis, Coracobrachialis; continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
MNEM.median: "The labourer's nerve" — supplies most forearm flexors and LOAF in the hand. Carpal tunnel → thenar wasting, numb lateral 3½ fingers. High injury → "hand of benediction".
MNEM.ulnar: "The musician's nerve" — fine finger movements (interossei). Funny bone at the medial epicondyle. Injury → claw hand of 4th & 5th fingers.
MNEM.radial: "BEST" muscles (Brachioradialis, Extensors, Supinator, Triceps). Spiral-groove fracture → wrist drop. Sensory: back of the hand / snuffbox.
MNEM.axillary: Through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery. Deltoid + teres minor. Regimental-badge numbness over lateral shoulder.
MNEM.long-thoracic: "C5-6-7 raise your wings to heaven" → winged scapula when injured (serratus anterior).
MNEM.phrenic: "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive." Descends on the front of anterior scalene. Referred pain to the shoulder tip.
MNEM.femoral: L2–L4. Femoral triangle "NAVeL" lateral → medial: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Lymphatics. Quadriceps + knee jerk.
MNEM.obturator: L2–L4 through the obturator foramen → medial (adductor) compartment of the thigh.
MNEM.sciatic: Largest nerve (L4–S3). Exits below piriformis. Divides above the knee into tibial (back) and common fibular (side). Inject the UPPER OUTER quadrant of the buttock to avoid it.
MNEM.tibial: Posterior leg and sole. Passes behind the medial malleolus ("Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry"). Injury → can't plantarflex or stand on tiptoe.
MNEM.common-fibular: Wraps the fibular neck — most commonly injured nerve of the lower limb (casts, crossed legs) → foot drop. "PED" = Peroneal Everts and Dorsiflexes; "TIP" = Tibial Inverts and Plantarflexes.
MNEM.superior-gluteal: Above piriformis → glute med, glute min, TFL. Injury = Trendelenburg gait.
MNEM.pudendal: S2–S4: "S2, 3, 4 keeps the poop off the floor" (external anal sphincter, pelvic floor).
MNEM.accessory: CN XI — trapezius + SCM. Test: shrug and turn the head against resistance.
MNEM.facial: Branches "To Zanzibar By Motor Car" = Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical.
MNEM.spinal-cord: 31 pairs of spinal nerves: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal ("Breakfast at 7, lunch at 12, dinner at 5" for C7/T12/L5 vertebrae count).
MNEM.thoracodorsal: Supplies latissimus dorsi ("thoraco-DORSAL to the DORSI"). Middle subscapular nerve.
MNEM.suprascapular: Supraspinatus + infraspinatus. Passes UNDER the superior transverse scapular ligament; the artery goes OVER ("Army over the bridge, Navy under").
MNEM.aorta: Arch branches "ABC'S": Aortic arch → Brachiocephalic trunk, left Common carotid, left Subclavian.
MNEM.subclavian-a: Branches "VIT C & D": Vertebral, Internal thoracic, Thyrocervical trunk, Costocervical trunk, Dorsal scapular.
MNEM.axillary-a: "Screw The Lawyer Save A Patient" = Superior thoracic | Thoracoacromial, Lateral thoracic | Subscapular, Anterior & Posterior circumflex humeral (parts 1 | 2 | 3 by pectoralis minor).
MNEM.brachial-a: Continuation of the axillary artery past teres major. Blood-pressure cuff + stethoscope in the cubital fossa. Cubital fossa medial → lateral "MBBR": Median nerve, Brachial artery, Biceps tendon, Radial nerve.
MNEM.radial-a: Pulse at the wrist lateral to the FCR tendon; runs through the anatomical snuffbox.
MNEM.external-carotid: Branches "Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students" = Superior thyroid, Ascending pharyngeal, Lingual, Facial, Occipital, Posterior auricular, Maxillary, Superficial temporal.
MNEM.celiac: "Left Hand Side" = Left gastric, Hepatic (common), Splenic.
MNEM.femoral-a: Femoral triangle "NAVeL" (Nerve, Artery, Vein, Lymphatics, lateral → medial). Pulse at the mid-inguinal point.
MNEM.popliteal-a: Deepest structure in the popliteal fossa (lies on the bone) — "NVA" from superficial to deep: Nerve, Vein, Artery.
MNEM.dorsalis-pedis: Pulse on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to the EHL tendon.
MNEM.post-tibial-a: Behind the medial malleolus — "Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry" (the A).
MNEM.great-saphenous: Longest vein in the body. Runs IN FRONT of the medial malleolus (reliable for a cut-down) and drains into the femoral vein at the saphenous opening. Harvested for bypass grafts.
MNEM.small-saphenous: Runs BEHIND the lateral malleolus and up the back of the calf to the popliteal vein.
MNEM.cephalic: "Cephalic is on the thumb side (lateral), Basilic on the Baby-finger side (medial)". Cephalic runs in the deltopectoral groove.
MNEM.basilic: "Basilic = Baby-finger side (medial)". Pierces deep fascia mid-arm to join the brachial veins → axillary vein.
MNEM.median-cubital: Joins cephalic → basilic across the cubital fossa — the usual vein for blood draws.
MNEM.internal-jugular: Runs in the carotid sheath with the common carotid artery and the vagus nerve ("I See 10 CC's in the IV": Internal jugular, CN X, Common Carotid).
MNEM.ivc: Passes through the diaphragm at T8 ("I 8 10 Eggs AT 12").
MNEM.azygos: "Azygos = unpaired" — drains the right posterior thoracic wall and arches over the right lung root into the SVC.
MNEM.portal-v: Formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the superior mesenteric + splenic veins. Carries gut blood to the liver.
